intro: Compare four ways an image can depart from familiar appearances. The strangeness can come from urban space, brushwork, spontaneous marks or the details of an individual life.
alt: An arcade with long shadows, a rough café scene, a field of floating marks and a direct portrait of Microsoft among symbolic objects.

variants.name: Metaphysical painting
variants.look: The nearly empty arcade and unnaturally long shadows turn a recognizable space into an uneasy one.
variants.history: In the 1910s, Giorgio de Chirico and others used empty piazzas and unexpected objects to give scenes an enigmatic atmosphere.
variants.when: Study how a recognizable place becomes strange when light, scale or familiar objects feel disconnected.
variants.why: An open space draws attention to every isolated object and shadow as possible clues.

variants.name: School of Paris
variants.look: The café figure has strongly colored contours and a rough surface against an oddly colored room.
variants.history: School of Paris is a loose label that has been applied to international artists who worked in Paris. Their many media and styles cannot be reduced to a common formula.
variants.when: Start with a named artist when using this label to orient your research.
variants.why: Knowing where artists worked can explain contact and exchange even when their pictures look very different.

variants.name: Abstract Surrealism
variants.look: Thin wandering marks and biomorphic shapes gather and disperse across the field.
variants.history: Surrealists experimented with automatic drawing and other processes that loosened deliberate control. Some of these works approach abstraction while others retain recognizable figures.
variants.when: Study how a mark or texture can start a sequence before the image's subject has been settled.
variants.why: The process allows visual associations to emerge gradually from placements, accidents and alterations.

variants.name: Kahlo and Mexican modernism
variants.look: A direct gaze and carefully selected objects make the portrait feel both literal and symbolic.
variants.history: Frida Kahlo made personal images within the diverse setting of Mexican modernism. Her work drew on specific experiences and Mexican visual practices, including small devotional paintings.
variants.when: Study particular works when you want to see how objects gain meaning through their relation to an individual's life.
variants.why: A steady portrait composition gives the viewer time to notice, and question, the meaning of the objects around the person.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: Metaphysical painting: half-empty urban arcade, sharp late light, extended shadows and mannequinesque silhouette with modern woman; School of Paris: expressionist urban café painting with rough paint touch and colored contours of modern woman, unusual ghost-blue ground; Abstract Surrealism: automatic drifting marks, biomorphic shapes and thin stringlike brushlines in floating field, modern woman as viewer; Kahlo and Mexican modernism: contemporary fictional artist-study portrait of unchanged modern ash-blonde woman before quiet leafy arch, direct gaze and personal symbolic office objects, no Kahlo facial traits and no copied composition. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
